title: Methodists
hookLine: John Wesley felt his heart strangely warmed (1738), and societies spread by horseback

cards: London, the evening of May 24, 1738. A small, tired Anglican priest named John Wesley goes, in his own words, very unwillingly, to a meeting in a room on Aldersgate Street.

He's thirty-four, just back from a mission to Georgia that went badly. He's been fasting, praying, working, and still feels no peace. Someone is reading aloud from Martin Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans.

Nothing dramatic. No music. And at about a quarter to nine, as he later wrote in his journal, while the reader was describing the change God works in the heart through faith, "I felt my heart strangely warmed."

teach.h: METHODIST: A JOKE ABOUT A METHOD.
teach.b: Methodist started as a joke. At Oxford, John Wesley, his brother Charles and a few friends had formed a little club that prayed, studied, fasted and visited prisoners on a strict schedule.
Other students mocked them as Methodists, for their method. The name stuck. After Aldersgate, Wesley took his warmed heart outdoors.
When churches closed their pulpits to him, he preached in fields, to coal miners at dawn, their faces black with soot. He spent decades on horseback, preaching wherever people would gather.

teach.h: HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?
teach.b: He gathered people into weekly small groups, called classes, that asked each other one question: how is it with your soul? Charles wrote a great many hymns, among them Hark! the Herald Angels Sing.

Wesley taught that God's grace doesn't only forgive; it changes you, and can grow a whole life toward love. He called it holiness of heart and life, and it spilled over into schools, clinics and the fight against slavery.
In America, circuit riders carried Methodism across the frontier on horseback. Wesley lived and died an Anglican priest; Methodists became their own churches after him.
There's an echo here of the road to Emmaus: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?"

teach.h: I FELT MY HEART STRANGELY WARMED.
teach.b: A heart warmed while someone opened the scriptures. And this week: the Catholic Church; Luther's hammer; Lutherans and the Reformed; Anglicans; Anabaptists; Baptists; and now the Methodists.
Seven days, each lit by something.

how: Methodists sing the Wesleys' hymns, many meet in small groups for prayer and accountability, and many Methodist churches celebrate Aldersgate Day on May 24.

games.q: you're John Wesley, and churches have closed their pulpits to you. what do you do?
o: preach outdoors, in fields, to anyone who comes.
games.why: Wesley preached in the open air, to coal miners at dawn and crowds in fields, and rode on horseback across Britain for decades.

practice: With a hand on your chest if you like, think of a moment when something unexpected moved you, a line in a song, a kindness from a stranger, words read aloud, and notice where you feel it in your body.
Then ask yourself Wesley's class question, quietly, taking your time: how is it with your soul? If you pray, ask God to warm your heart; if you don't, just listen for the answer.

wordCard.voice: Methodists. The movement of John and Charles Wesley: a warmed heart, small groups, hymns, and grace that changes a life.
